title: When do the stars come out after sunset?
subtitle: Crossing the three stages of twilight with your own eyes
intro: The Sun going down does not bring the stars out at once. It takes another hour and a half for the sky to go fully dark, and that stretch falls into three stages. Knowing them before you go out saves you a wasted trip.

steps.title: Just before sunset
steps.text:
The western sky. The Sun is hanging 3 degrees above the horizon and will be down shortly.

For the sake of the explanation this lesson has set the observing site to an autumn evening at 37.5°N, so that the whole run of twilight can be watched from beginning to end. At the last step it returns to where you are.

There is not a single star in the sky yet. To be exact, the stars are up there in the daytime too, but the sky is too bright and they are buried in it. The air scatters sunlight in every direction.

Stars begin to show because the sky darkens, not because the stars come up.

steps.title: Sunset — civil twilight begins here
steps.text:
18:40. The Sun has gone below the horizon. From this moment twilight begins.

The Sun is gone and the sky is still bright. From below the horizon it is lighting the upper atmosphere, and that light scatters down to us.

This first stage is called civil twilight, running from a solar altitude of 0 degrees to -6 degrees. Its marks are clear.

  • It is bright enough to read a book outdoors
  • The street lights begin to come on
  • Only the one or two brightest things show in the sky: a planet such as Venus, or a star of the class of Sirius

What get called 'evening stars' appear in this stretch. They show not because it is dark but because they are exceptionally bright.

steps.title: End of civil twilight — the first-magnitude stars
steps.text:
19:07. The solar altitude is -6 degrees. Civil twilight ends and nautical twilight begins.

The western horizon is still bright, but overhead it has darkened a good deal. The first-magnitude stars appear one after another.

The order in which the stars appear is the order of their brightness. As the sky darkens the brightest beat the background first and the rest follow. The magnitudes from 'What brightness means' are laid out in front of you in order.

East Asian astronomy called the time after sunset hon (昏) and the time before sunrise sin (晨). The star standing in the middle of the southern sky at hon, the honjungseong, was used to fix the solar terms. In an age without clocks, twilight was both the scale of the day and the scale of the year.

steps.title: End of nautical twilight — the sea horizon goes
steps.text:
19:37. The solar altitude is -12 degrees. Nautical twilight ends and astronomical twilight begins.

The origin of the name is worth knowing. Up to the end of this stage the horizon at sea is still visible. That stretch, with stars and the sea horizon both in view, was a sailor's only chance to fix a position with a sextant, because measuring the altitude of a star needs a visible horizon to measure it from.

Past this stage the horizon sinks into the dark and can no longer be made out. Hence nautical twilight.

Stars down to magnitude 2 or 3 are out now and the shapes of the constellations can be made out. Some faint brightness still lingers in the west, though.

steps.title: End of astronomical twilight — real night
steps.text:
20:10. The solar altitude is -18 degrees. Twilight is over. From here on is what astronomers call night.

Every trace of the Sun's light has gone and the sky will get no darker. Only now do the following become possible.

  • The Milky Way comes out
  • Faint nebulae and galaxies can be seen
  • You can count down to magnitude 6

Getting here from sunset took an hour and a half. If you went out to see the Andromeda Galaxy, this is where it starts. It is worth arriving before then, to buy time for your eyes to settle into the dark.

quiz.q: What only becomes possible once astronomical twilight has ended?
opts: Making out the shapes of the constellations
Observing the Milky Way and faint nebulae
quiz.explain: First-magnitude stars come out around the end of civil twilight, and the shapes of the constellations can be made out during nautical twilight. Faint light spread over a wide area, such as the Milky Way, only separates from the background once the sky itself is fully dark. The Moon is bright enough to be seen in broad daylight.

steps.title: Twilight depends on the season and the latitude
steps.text:
Twilight is not always the same length. It depends on how steeply the Sun crosses the horizon.

  • The equator — the Sun goes down almost vertically. Twilight is short, a little over an hour, and darkness follows sunset quickly
  • Middle latitudes — around an hour and a half, as we have just watched. Longer in summer
  • High latitudes — the Sun goes down at a very shallow angle and twilight runs for hours. In summer it never reaches -18 degrees and night never comes at all. That is the midnight sun

North of 48.5°N, astronomical twilight does not end at midsummer. Paris and Vancouver are around that line, and London and Berlin have no real night through the whole of June. Observers there rest in summer and work in winter.

Between 33 and 38°N, which covers Korea and southern Japan, night does come even at midsummer. In late June, though, the end of astronomical twilight is pushed back to close to 10 pm.

steps.title: How long the eye takes to adapt
steps.text:
The sky going dark and your eyes getting used to the dark are two different stories.

  • The pupil widens in a few seconds
  • The light-sensitive chemistry of the retina recovers over 20 to 30 minutes
  • Full adaptation can take as long as 45 minutes

Once adapted, the sensitivity of the eye rises more than 10,000 times. The number of stars visible in the same sky doubles or trebles.

The trouble is that one bright light puts you back to the beginning. A single look at a phone screen returns you to where you were minutes ago.

So observers use red light. The rods of a dark-adapted retina are least sensitive to red, so you can read a map and keep your adaptation. Byeolmuri has a night mode as well. It covers the whole screen in red to protect your eyes when you have it out with you.

quiz.q: Why do observers use red light in the field?
opts: Because a dark-adapted eye is least sensitive to red, so less of the adaptation is lost
Because red light does not mix with starlight
quiz.explain: The rods that do the work in the dark have low sensitivity at the red end of the spectrum. So under a red light you can read a map without losing much of your dark adaptation. It is a way of not throwing away, with one flash of white light, the adaptation that took 20 to 30 minutes to build.

steps.title: Make a plan for tonight
steps.text:
The observing site is back to where you are. Now it is time to plan tonight.

  • Open the 'Tonight' tab and it gives you today's times for sunset, the end of twilight, the start of twilight and sunrise, along with how many hours of darkness there are
  • If you are after the faint things — the Milky Way, nebulae, galaxies — go out so as to arrive after astronomical twilight ends
  • If it is only the Moon, the planets and bright stars, civil twilight will do. A crescent Moon and Venus are in fact more beautiful while the sky is still blue
  • Once you arrive, wait 20 minutes. Not looking at your phone in that time decides how the night goes
  • While twilight runs, count the order in which the stars appear. Remember which one comes out first and you can guess its magnitude

credits: The solar-altitude limits of the twilight stages (-6, -12 and -18 degrees) follow the international standard, and the times on screen were read directly from the engine for 37.5°N on 15 September 2026.
